title: Two Big Leaders Meet: Xi and Trump Agree on AI Hotline
summary: Imagine two of the biggest countries in the world — the United States and China — sitting down for a three-day meeting in Washington, D.C. That's exactly what happened. President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping shook hands and agreed to set up a special hotline for AI problems. If something goes wrong with artificial intelligence, the two countries can talk fast instead of guessing. They also agreed to keep talking about their armies, so small problems don't turn into big ones. On trade, they agreed to keep a two-month pause on some tariffs (taxes on goods that travel between countries). China even said it will buy at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the U.S. in 2027 and 2028. That's a lot of coal — about the weight of 100,000 school buses! Trump said the U.S. won't slow down its AI work. "We're leading by at least a year," he told reporters. The two sides will meet again in Shenzhen, China, in November. No giant breakthroughs, but experts say the new hotlines are a big deal.
why_it_matters: When the world's two biggest countries agree to talk quickly instead of guessing, it can keep arguments — and prices at the store — from getting out of hand where you live.

background_read: The United States and China are the two biggest economies in the world, so when their leaders meet, it matters for people everywhere.
President Xi Jinping (China's top leader) and President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) sat down together in Washington, D.C. (the capital city of the United States).

Countries have used special 'hotlines' before: after a very scary moment in 1962 called the Cuban Missile Crisis, the U.S. and the Soviet Union set up a direct line so leaders could talk quickly and avoid big mistakes.
Article_Structure: WHO: President Donald Trump of the United States and President Xi Jinping of China.
WHAT: They agreed to set up a special hotline for AI problems, keep talking about their armies, hold a two-month pause on some tariffs, and China said it will buy coal from the U.S.
WHERE: A three-day meeting in Washington, D.C., with the next meeting set for Shenzhen, China, in November.
WHY: So the two countries can talk fast if something goes wrong with AI, and so small problems do not grow into big ones.

perspectives.description: Supporters say the new hotlines mean the two biggest countries can catch trouble early, so a mistake with AI or with armies does not turn into a real fight.
Critics point out there were no giant breakthroughs: the coal deal and the tariff pause are only temporary, and the two sides still disagree about many big things.
Experts see this as slow, careful diplomacy — setting up ways to talk is useful even when a meeting does not solve everything.
